Case Vignette: "Raj"

Raj is a 35-year-old married South Asian man who works as a tax consultant. He presents for therapy at his wife's urging, though he is not entirely sure what he hopes to gain. He speaks in a measured, deliberate tone, often pausing to search for the right word, as if translating thoughts from another language.

Three years ago, Raj volunteered with an international relief organization in a conflict zone in the Middle East. He had always been a quiet, competent man, good with numbers and logistics. His job was to manage supply chains for a field hospital-ensuring antibiotics, bandages, and surgical kits arrived where they were needed. He was proud of the work. He felt useful.

The event that changed him happened on a Tuesday afternoon. A convoy of aid trucks had been delayed at a checkpoint. Raj was in the back office of the hospital, reviewing inventory on a laptop, when the first shell hit. He remembers the sound not as a boom but as a physical force-a wall of air that threw him out of his chair. The lights went out. Dust filled his throat. When he opened his eyes, he was on the floor, and the world was silent for a moment, then filled with screams.

He crawled through the dark toward the emergency exit. He found a young nurse, a woman named Leila, pinned under a collapsed shelving unit. Her leg was twisted beneath her. He tried to lift the metal frame, but it wouldn't budge. He shouted for help, but no one came. He held her hand. He told her it would be okay. He watched her eyes go from terror to something else-a quiet, glassy stillness. He does not know if she died in that moment or later. He could not stay. The building was on fire. He left her.

He made it out. He was evacuated two days later. He returned home to his wife, his office, his spreadsheets. He did not tell her the full story. He said it was "rough." He went back to work within two weeks.

Now, three years later, Raj cannot sit in a restaurant without scanning the exits. He cannot drive past a construction site with a jackhammer without his heart racing. He has not been to a movie theater since he returned-the darkness, the enclosed space, the sudden loud noises from the screen-it feels too close. At work, he is still competent, but he has become rigid. He double-checks every number three times. He cannot tolerate surprise. His colleagues think he is meticulous; his wife knows he is afraid.

He wakes most nights around 3:00 a.m. with his jaw clenched and his sheets soaked. He does not remember dreams, only a sense of falling. He avoids the news. He avoids documentaries. He avoids any mention of the region where he served. When a client mentions a charity donation, Raj feels a cold sweat at the back of his neck. He changes the subject.

His wife says he is "not present." She says he is there but not there. He knows she is right. He feels like he is watching his own life from a great distance, a man going through motions that no longer feel real. He has stopped laughing. He has stopped arguing. He has stopped feeling much of anything except a low, constant hum of vigilance.

When asked what he wants from therapy, Raj is quiet for a long time. He looks at his hands. "I want to stop seeing her face," he says. "I want to stop feeling like I'm still in that room."
